summary:
PathogenBreak is a decision-support tool that helps farmers in Indore, Madhya Pradesh choose crop rotations that protect soil health, conserve water and adapt to changing conditions. Indore is sliding into a soybean–wheat monoculture: government data shows gram (chickpea) area fell 89% since 2019 while wheat rose 56%. Growing the same hosts every year lets soil-borne fungi build up and increases groundwater use.

Our tool combines NASA Earth observations (NASA POWER temperature, rainfall, humidity and soil wetness; GPM IMERG rainfall; MODIS EVI) with local soil data, crop statistics, pathogen databases and a low-cost soil-moisture sensor. It scores 256 feasible two-year rotations on crop fit, disease carry-over, nitrogen benefit and irrigation need, and stress-tests them across 13 real years plus drought, flood and heat scenarios. Farmers pick their priority (break disease, keep income or save water) and get one clear action for today, in English or Hindi. The strongest option cuts disease carry-over by 45% and saves 200 mm of irrigation per hectare.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

PathogenBreak answers the question an Indore farmer faces every November: "My monsoon crop is harvested — what should I sow now?" The farmer selects the crop just harvested, their priority, and the soil-moisture reading from our sensor. The app returns one clear action (for example "SOW GRAM now" or "WAIT – do not sow, the field is waterlogged"), the two-year plan behind it, expected income versus today, and irrigation need. The same message can be sent to an LCD display in the field (prototype hardware). Live app: https://pathogenbreak.streamlit.app

HOW IT WORKS

1. Season climate from NASA POWER (2013–2026) and GPM IMERG rainfall for 13 complete crop years.

2. Crop suitability for 10 local crops from rainfall, temperature, soil pH and black-clay waterlogging (SoilGrids).

3. Disease carry-over between crops from USDA Fungus-Host records and PHI-base gene-level evidence, graded by evidence strength; soil-borne fungi weigh most.

4. Hard crop-calendar rules remove 369 impossible sequences (e.g. mustard after cotton).

5. An uncertainty engine tests every plan in 13 real years plus drought, excess-rain and heat scenarios, and labels it Recommend, Qualify or Withhold. A sensitivity test across 81 weight settings checks robustness.

6. A farmer check adds irrigation need and net income at 2026-27 MSP and Indore mandi prices.

7. The live sensor reading is ranked against 13 years of NASA soil wetness for the same month to decide dry / normal / wet / waterlogged.

RESULTS (Indore, normal year)

- Keep income: Maize → Wheat → Soybean → Wheat — disease −17%, income −2%.

- Strongest break: Maize → Gram → Soybean → Wheat — disease −45%, irrigation 300 mm vs 500 mm, wins in 16/16 scenarios and 81/81 weight settings; income −21% at MSP.

- Save water: Soybean → Lentil → Maize → Gram — irrigation 70 mm.

- Pilot plot: Groundnut → Mustard → Soybean → Wheat — disease −54%, income +2%.

VALIDATION AND HONESTY

NASA Rabi water correlates with real Indore wheat production (r = 0.51) and MODIS greenness with wheat output (r = 0.42); MODIS confirms the crop calendar. Across 55 Madhya Pradesh districts, repeating a crop goes with slightly lower next-year yields (−2.0% for soybean) — the right direction but not statistically significant, so a field trial is our next step. We show trade-offs openly instead of hiding them.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Healthier soil, up to 2,000 m³ of groundwater saved per hectare, and a choice the farmer understands — on a phone, in Hindi, with a low-cost sensor.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, NumPy, matplotlib), Jupyter, Streamlit (web app), GitHub, Arduino with LM393 soil-moisture probe, HC-05 Bluetooth and 16×2 I2C LCD.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a single "best" answer, PathogenBreak links NASA climate data, pathogen genetics and farmer economics, and lets the farmer choose the trade-off. A live sensor makes the advice specific to their own field.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Crop calendar feasibility, local farming experience, groundwater use, income at MSP and market prices, climate variability, evidence quality of pathogen records, and accessibility (Hindi, simple interface).

USE OF SI

An AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) was used to help write and debug the analysis code and app, design the slides, translate the app into Hindi, and draft text. Data selection, testing and decisions were made by the team. No photos or illustrations were AI-generated; all charts are plotted from real data by our code, and app screenshots are real.
